text:

Objet : Vulnérabilité dans OpenSSH

Gestion du document

Titre
Vulnérabilité dans OpenSSH

Date de la première version05 novembre 2026

Date de la dernière version05 novembre 2026

Source(s)
Bulletin de sécurité OpenSSH release-10.6p2 du 05 novembre 2026

Une gestion de version détaillée se trouve à la fin de ce document.

Risque

Contournement de la politique de sécurité

Systèmes affectés

OpenSSH versions antérieures à 10.6p2

Résumé
Le 5 novembre 2026, OpenSSH a publié un avis de sécurité concernant une vulnérabilité qui permet à un attaquant de contourner l’authentification d'un service SSH.
En effet, sur les systèmes Linux qui utilisent la bibliothèque standard C musl, compilés sans support PAM ou avec PAM désactivé, un attaquant peut se connecter en fournissant deux mots de passe, dont le deuxième est d'une longueur strictement supérieure à 256 caractères et inférieure à 1024.
Lorsque les conditions sont réunies, cette vulnérabilité est triviale à exploiter. Il convient donc de vérifier si le système est dans une configuration vulnérable.
Indicateurs de compromission
Le chercheur, qui a découvert la vulnérabilité, recommande de vérifier la légitimité des connexions de chaque compte système avec une étoile (:*:) (mot de passe désactivé) dans /etc/shadow. Par exemple, la commande suivante peut être lancée en root :
awk -F : '$2 == "*" {print $1}' /etc/shadow | xargs -r -I{} grep "Accepted password for {}" /var/log/messages
Mesure de contournement
Il est préférable de désactiver l'authentification par mot de passe ou, à défaut, de désactiver le service, si l'application du correctif est impossible.

Solutions

title: CVE-2026-58273 - Rucio: Authorisation Bypass on REST API endpoint for signing URLs
text:
8.8

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-58273
Rucio: Authorisation Bypass on REST API endpoint for signing URLs

Rucio is a scientific data management framework. From 1.16.1 until 35.9.0, 38.6.0, and 41.0.0rc1, the /credentials/signurl endpoint reads X-Rucio-Account instead of the account stored in request.environ['issuer'] by token authentication. Any authenticated low-privilege user can supply root as the header value and pass the root-only get_signed_url permission check. The server then returns a presigned read, write, or delete URL for an attacker-selected object using stored S3, GCS, or Swift credentials, and X-Rucio-VO can select another tenant in multi-VO deployments. This permits data disclosure, modification, deletion, and cross-tenant access on cloud-backed RSEs. This issue is fixed in versions 35.9.0, 38.6.0, and 41.0.0rc1.

CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-33944
Dolibarr: SQL Injection in societe/class/societe.class.php via localtax1_value parameter

Dolibarr is an open-source enterprise resource planning and customer relationship management application. Prior to 22.0.5 and 23.0.1, there is a SQL injection vulnerability in the Third Party company update functionality. The application concatenates the  localtax1_value  and  localtax2_value  properties into an SQL UPDATE statement without numeric conversion or other appropriate sanitization. An authenticated user with Third Party create or edit permission can submit crafted  lt1  or  lt2  POST parameters to read sensitive database information, including password hashes, API keys, and business data, or modify third-party records. This issue is fixed in versions 22.0.5 and 23.0.2.

text: Jai Vijayan,Contributing WriterNovember 5, 20264 Min ReadSource: tete_escape via Shutterstock It has emerged this week that Russia's APT29 threat group compromised the website of a Ukrainian SEO and website analytics service, and briefly used the access to distribute malicious device-fingerprinting code to potentially thousands of iPhone and Android users.The weeklong compromise earlier this year was part of a broader watering-hole campaign from APT29 (aka Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard, and The Dukes) that also used other legitimate and fake websites to distribute the fingerprinting malware, and later to collect sensitive personal information from selected devices.No Clear Cyberattack Targeting, Beyond Android & iPhone UsersResearchers at Sekoia who are tracking the campaign are unsure if the state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) had specific targets in mind, or if it was simply trying to infect as many vulnerable phones as possible."Across the directly compromised websites, no single sectoral targeting pattern emerges from our analysis," Sekoia's threat research and intelligence team wrote. "While the victimology shows a focus on Ukraine and the United States, the inclusion of unrelated entities such as an Australian medical clinic complicates a broad strategic interpretation." APT29 is a familiar threat actor that the US government has formally tied to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Its primary mission is intelligence gathering on behalf of Moscow, with a focus on government agencies, diplomatic organizations, think tanks, technology companies, healthcare, and research institutions. Among its most prominent campaigns were the breaches at the Democratic National Committee in 2016, efforts to steal COVID-19 vaccine research in 2020, and the SolarWinds supply-chain compromise, which gave it access to numerous US government agencies and private-sector organizations. The group is known for stealthy, long-term intrusions, and in recent years has increasingly targeted cloud environments, email accounts, and technology providers to gain access to downstream victims.3 Different APT29 Infection VectorsIn its latest campaign, APT29 used three separate infection vectors to target iOS and Android devices. One involved compromising legitimate websites and injecting malicious JavaScript that exposed visitors to a device-fingerprinting script. Among the websites the threat actor turned into watering holes were those of a US chemical-industry trade association, a Ukrainian gas producer, and a Bulgarian military-related organization.When unable to compromise a legitimate website, the group created lookalike domains that impersonated the real sites, and modified their content in real-time to inject the malicious code. Two examples it impersonated were the America250 national celebration website and London's Raffles hotel. The third vector involved a supply chain compromise of Ukrainian website analytics firm Plerdy. According to Sekoia, thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian, use the company's tracking scripts. By injecting malicious code into that script, APT29 potentially exposed visitors to those sites to its device-fingerprinting and exploit-delivery infrastructure, Sekoia said.The fingerprinting malware collected device and browser data from Android and iOS devices and sent it to an APT29 command-and-control service, which then delivered one of three different exploit chains depending on the mobile platform and browser/OS versions. Attackers can log in to accounts that have no password, such as SSH key-only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers running the standard openssh-server package. They need network access to the server, an account name, and a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long.

OpenSSH, which rates the flaw critical, released version 10.6p2 today to block it. Alpine has published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16.

The attack works when the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks passwords without the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface, password logins are enabled, and at least one other account on the machine has a password. Alpine's openssh-server package is built without PAM, and password logins are on by default.

The flaw comes from how sshd works with musl, the C library that Alpine is built on. Non-Linux systems, Linux systems built on glibc, and systems that check passwords through PAM are not affected, said Damien Miller of the OpenSSH project.

He told anyone running an affected system to "set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY." No attacks using the flaw have been reported.

Who Is Exposed

Alpine's security advisory lists four conditions. A server is exposed when all four are true:

It runs the openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or runs openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no.
PasswordAuthentication is yes, which is the OpenSSH default.
An account has * as its password field, which means no password is set.
At least one other local account has a password hash starting with $5$ or $6$.

The attacker also needs the name of an account with no password. One account with a password is enough to expose every account without one. The attack succeeds on every try with a single connection, according to the advisory.

On Alpine, accounts with no password set include:

key-only users created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*'
users who come from a directory service through musl-nscd, since they have no shadow entry
root, which has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16
the alpine user in the official cloud images built with tiny-cloud

Root is protected by the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password setting and can be reached directly only if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That protection does not help if an exposed account can become root, for example through doas.

The tiny-cloud images from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 give the alpine user passwordless doas. They are safe at first boot but become open to attack once any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example after an admin sets a console password. An attacker can then log in as alpine and use doas to become root.

Containers that do not run sshd, systems with PasswordAuthentication no, and cloud images set up through cloud-init, which writes that setting, are not affected. Accounts locked with ! in /etc/shadow are not affected either, and neither are machines where no account has a $-style password hash.

The flaw is not limited to Alpine. Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield, who reported it, names OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto in his technical write-up as other musl-based systems to check.

OpenWrt handles SSH with Dropbear by default, as its Dropbear documentation shows, and Kültekin says Dropbear is not affected. On OpenWrt, the flaw can matter only where an admin has installed the OpenSSH server.

How to Fix It

On Alpine, the fix is a package update followed by a restart, because upgrading the package does not restart the running sshd:

Update the packages: apk upgrade -U -a
Restart the server: rc-service sshd restart

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability that could be exploited to bypass Lockdown Mode protections in OpenAI ChatGPT.

Lockdown Mode was introduced by the artificial intelligence (AI) company in June 2026 as an optional setting to minimize data exfiltration risks arising from prompt injections.

"The flaw could enable silent chat data theft, phishing, and malware delivery, including zero-click data exfiltration in the ChatGPT desktop application," Eli Smadja, head of research at Check Point, said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The problem stems from HTML page previews inside ChatGPT code blocks, which allow HTML content to be rendered directly within the application. Given that executing user-supplied HTML and JavaScript can introduce security risks of its own, the content is placed inside a sandbox so that it cannot access data from the app, such as cookies and local storage.

The sandbox also prevents the rendered content from communicating with external resources without user consent. Lockdown Mode acts as a security barrier, mitigating data exfiltration risk by limiting outbound network requests that could be used to transfer sensitive information to an attacker-controlled infrastructure.

However, Check Point found a loophole in the manner popup windows are handled during HTML previews that made it possible to escape the confines of the sandbox and bypass Lockdown Mode.

"The HTML preview used nested sandboxed frames, and while ChatGPT intercepted direct attempts to open new windows, the underlying sandbox permissions still allowed popups and permitted them to escape the sandbox," Smadja explained.

"By creating another nested frame within the rendered page, it was possible to access an unmodified popup function and bypass the restrictions placed on the original HTML preview. Content opened through this route was no longer subject to the same sandbox restrictions, providing a way to circumvent the protections of Lockdown Mode."

Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat.

What's more, as the attacker is in complete control of the content displayed in the popup window, it could be used to render convincing social-engineering lures, such as a fake ChatGPT update, and trick the victim into downloading malware by persuading them to click on a link.

That said, the underlying issue is not limited to the Electron-based desktop environment, highlighting how weakness outside of the scope of the AI model can undermine AI security controls. Following responsible disclosure, the vulnerability was addressed by OpenAI on September 18, 2026.

"Lockdown Mode was specifically intended to reduce the possibility of data leaving a conversation through potentially malicious outbound requests, yet a weakness in another application feature provided an alternative path around that security boundary," Smadja said.

"The finding raises a broader enterprise security issue: AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them."

The disclosure comes a week after Parameter Labs detailed a way to bypass ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy (CSP) and take over anyone's account simply by sending an attacker-controlled public ChatGPT share link and prompting them to click the HTML preview once. Even a simple file copy can reach places it shouldn't. And while new tools are helping find security holes faster, some important systems are still taking months, sometimes over a year, to get patched. Not exactly a great match.

The stranger part is how little some attacks now need. Ransom demands without encrypted files. Fake websites that look real enough to steal money. AI tools picking up dangerous instructions while trying to help. Even the attackers are making mistakes in their own code.

AI Accelerates Zero-Day Discovery

NCSC Warns of AI-Enabled Attacks

The U.K. National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) has warned that the widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has "almost certainly" led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. "Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and have made patching a quicker process," NCSC said. "However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal."

Critical Systems Face Prolonged Exposure

An analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026 has found that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. title: How Adversaries Are Turning the Vulnerability Ecosystem Against Defenders
text:
How Adversaries Are Turning the Vulnerability Ecosystem Against Defenders
CrowdStrike’s analysis of vulnerability weaponization timelines reveals adversaries are quickly adopting public vulnerability research, often within hours.

November 05, 2026
•

Lacie Blythe - Jaime Duque
•

Threat Hunting & Intel

The security community has long operated on a foundational belief: Sharing knowledge makes everyone safer. Researchers publish technical blogs, release proof-of-concept (POC) code, and distribute scanning templates to help defenders understand vulnerabilities, prioritize patching, and build better detections. This belief is not wrong, but it is incomplete. 
The same public research that helps defenders understand a vulnerability also hands adversaries a roadmap to exploit it. Analysis of weaponization timelines that CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations observed between January 2026 and July 2026 reinforces that in 2026, adversaries are rapidly adopting public vulnerability research, often within hours. 
The Window Is Closing
Public vulnerability research (security advisories, technical blogs, scanning templates, and POC and exploit code) is available to everyone, including adversaries.
The data from the first half of 2026 makes clear how threat actors are using it. Analyzing in-the-wild exploitation CrowdStrike has observed between January and July 2026, the median time from when a vulnerability had a public POC to when threat actors exploited it was less than one day, with the fastest observed exploitation after a public POC being 35 minutes. Of the vulnerabilities with a public POC that CrowdStrike saw threat actors exploit, 91 percent were exploited within 48 hours of POC release.
POC publication is the race’s green flag. For organizations operating on traditional patch cycles, the window to act before exploitation begins has effectively closed. The question defenders need to ask is whether they are able to patch before exploitation begins. For most organizations operating on traditional patch cycles, the honest answer is no.
Public research benefits threat actors at every skill level. Less-skilled threat actors gain easily or fully weaponized POCs and exploitation guidance that put previously out-of-reach vulnerabilities within their grasp; highly skilled threat actors eliminate redundant development work, reduce costs, and improve operational security by blending in with the broader exploitation noise. 
Regardless of sophistication, the outcome is the same: faster operationalization, broader reach, and significantly reduced investment.
What This Looks Like in Practice
cPanel Authentication Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2026-41940)
On April 28, 2026, cPanel disclosed the authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-41940, which affects select versions of cPanel and WebHost Manager (WHM) and WordPress Squared (WP2). An unauthenticated remote attacker can leverage CVE-2026-41940 to gain unauthorized access to the control panels for these programs. 
A day later, on April 29, 2026, a well-known industry firm published a technical blog post that provided detailed exploitation guidance for CVE-2026-41940 and a purported detection-artifact generator to detect vulnerable instances.1 CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations analyzed the purported detection-artifact generator and determined that it simply requires a minor modification. Attackers need only to un-comment a line of code that changes the root password, and then the attacker can log in to the WHM terminal as the root user, essentially making the purported detection-artifact generator a weaponized exploit.
On April 30, 2026, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations began to observe widespread and opportunistic exploitation of CVE-2026-41940. Most if not all of the observed exploitation matched the exploitation guidance provided in the technical blog and/or purported detection artifact generator.

Zyxel GS1900 network switches that received the vendor's earlier fix for an actively exploited flaw are still open to the exploit attackers used, researchers at Binarly found.

The exploit lets anyone who can reach a switch's web management interface run commands on it without logging in. Zyxel has released new firmware for 10 GS1900 models that closes the hole.

The earlier fix is the 2.90 Patch 2 firmware, named in a June 16 advisory for a flaw tracked as CVE-2026-7273. The new 2.90 Patch 3 firmware fixes a flaw now tracked separately as CVE-2026-107441, which the exploit relies on. It was posted on October 23, and the vendor announced it in an advisory earlier this week.

The researchers, who reported the flaw to the vendor on September 29, call it a zero-day. Attackers already had a working exploit for it by then.

GreyNoise, which monitors attack traffic through a network of sensors, reported on September 21 that attackers took data from 996 GS1900 switches around August 17. It tied the attacks to CVE-2026-7273, and the researchers say the exploit it described matches the one they found.

Neither GreyNoise nor Binarly says the attacked switches were running the earlier fix, and the vendor's advisory does not say whether the new flaw has been exploited.

Switches on Patch 2 or any earlier firmware need the Patch 3 build for their model. The builds are posted with their firmware release notes.

The advisory lists no workaround for owners who cannot update yet. It also does not say whether updating removes access an attacker may already have, or what owners should check if a switch may have been compromised.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 21 and gave federal agencies until September 24 to apply the vendor's fix, the Patch 2 firmware. GluonTS is an open-source Python library for probabilistic time series modeling.

We identified CVE-2026-119083, an issue in the archive extraction utility in GluonTS before 0.17.0. An actor who supplies a crafted tar archive containing symbolic or hard links might be able to write arbitrary files outside the intended extraction directory with the privileges of the extracting process.

Impacted versions: < 0.17.0

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in gluonts version 0.17.0. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, do not use GluonTS to extract tar archives from untrusted or unverified sources. Anti-Malware Research

16 min read

GhostMap: The Android flaw that crashes your phone before you open the app
Alecsandru Cătălin DAJ

November 05, 2026
Promo Protect all your devices, without slowing them down. Free 30-day trial Bitdefender Labs researchers found that installing a specially crafted app can leave an Android phone stuck in a crash loop, even if you never open it or grant it a single permission. The app contains no code and never needs to run.  After installation, a core system process crashes, restarts, and crashes again, leaving the phone stuck in a boot loop. Restarting doesn't help, and neither does safe mode.  To get the phone working again, you need a factory reset, which erases the user's data. If, by chance, USB debugging had already been enabled, you could use a computer with ADB (Android Debug Bridge) to delete the file before the phone reboots. We began investigating on Aug. 12, 2026, when an APK collected from the wild crashed emulators in our analysis infrastructure. The sample was a banking dropper that never ran and crashed during installation.  When we looked closer to find out why, we found the problem wasn't the malware—it was the Android itself. The operating system mishandles two fields inside a ZIP entry, the compression method and the declared uncompressed length. Reading such an entry causes a SIGBUS (a signal sent by the CPU to stop a process that accesses an invalid memory space) in whichever process touches the file.  We call it GhostMap: the malformed entry causes Android to map the file across memory that was never allocated, and the crash occurs when a process reads from that empty space. Based on our testing, we consider the risk posed by this bug to be significant. In theory, an attacker could hide this technique in a fake app to disable a victim’s phone, or use the threat of a factory reset and data loss as leverage for extortion. Malformed APKs could also disrupt tools that inspect Android applications. We have not observed any of these scenarios in the wild. Key findings 
An app you never open can render your phone unusable. Simply installing the crafted app is enough to trigger the crash loop. It requests no permissions and contains no executable code.
Restarting the phone doesn’t solve the problem. The crash loop persists after a reboot and continues in safe mode. Restoring the phone may require a factory reset, which erases locally stored data.
Running on the latest Android version. Researchers reproduced the failure on a Pixel 10 running Android 17 with the Aug. 5, 2026 security patch. It affects all Android versions from Android 10 and above.
The discovery began with an APK found in the wild. It crashed Bitdefender’s analysis emulators, prompting the investigation. Researchers later developed a demonstration of the persistent crash loop.
Google assessed the issue as outside the scope of a security fix. Bitdefender reported the findings on Aug. 20 and Aug. 25, 2026. According to Google’s second response, the issue will not be addressed through a security update and was referred to a feature team for possible consideration in a future version.

The banking dropper was wrapped by a packer. This is a tool that rewrites an APK's internal structure so reverse-engineering tools can't read it. It’s very common in modern Android malware.  In this case, the same rewrite also broke the Android component that parses an app during installation. That’s why the installation crashed in the first place and why our emulators failed on it. The good news is that nothing in the sample suggests the author knew the file would crash anything. The sample did no more than that—a failed install. The underlying flaw runs deeper. We found that the same mistake can be aimed at a core system service instead of the installer, and there it produces the repeating crash loop described above, with no way back except a factory reset. That escalation is our own work; we have not seen it used against […]

title: Hacking on Autopilot: Inside ARTEX Cybercrime Campaigns
text:
Hacking on Autopilot: Inside ARTEX Cybercrime Campaigns

November 5, 2026

Key Points

Agentic hacking platforms like ARTEX, where AI models autonomously drive vulnerability discovery and exploitation, have been observed to be used by various cyber criminals.

Check Point Research’s analysis of the current landscape observed more than 1,800 publicly exposed instances for ARTEX alone, showing a massive scale of deployments.

While previous threat reports on ARTEX focused on the observed telemetry on the victim side, we present artifacts from the operator consoles. This data shows which models were used as well as how the operators prompted their agents.

Most attacks were fully autonomous besides the initial goal setup. Threat actors barely interacted with their agent fleets.

In the observed activity, Chinese models are most prevalent, with Deepseek Flash taking the lead. Operators mostly only interacted with their agents to check the progress of the current operations – attacks were almost fully autonomous.

The goals set by the attackers were exclusively to carry out opportunistic, financially motivated cybercrime, mostly on a broad scale. Agents abused various web vulnerabilities, such as Remote Code Execution (RCE), to achieve their goals. In some cases, agents were using the access gained to actively carry out supply chain attacks.

Introduction

ARTEX is a Chinese open-source, AI-powered penetration testing platform designed to help security teams assess systems they own or are authorized to test. It uses large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multiple AI agents that plan tests, run security tools, and record evidence of potential vulnerabilities. Its web dashboard brings together assets, testing progress, captured traffic, and findings, allowing users to monitor activity and guide the agents. By linking each investigation to specific assets and supporting vulnerability retesting, ARTEX aims to reduce repetitive work while keeping human oversight central to the testing process.

After the tool was observed in attacks against South Korean banks, its developer decided to make the project closed-source on October 8th. However, various maintained forks and backups of the original repository keep the tool publicly available to threat actors.

Figure 1 – ARTEX Panel.

As described further below, artifacts obtained by Check Point Research show that these systems can work fully autonomously after the initial goal has been set by the operator. Using agentic hacking frameworks like ARTEX, threat actors can carry out attacks at a previously impossible speed, on a broad scale and without any technical knowledge, opening the field to a large set of people.

Besides ARTEX, other frameworks such as CyberStrike, Cairn or PentAGI offer similar capabilities. Check Point Research also observed various other custom agentic hacking frameworks in the wild. While some of these are based on open-source tools such as those mentioned above, others are written from the ground up.

Figure 2 – Custom agentic hacking framework “PZZ”.

While many ARTEX instances are hidden behind firewalls or are set up in local networks, threat actors often expose administrative interfaces to the internet, to make them accessible remotely. Check Point Research found 2,557 systems hosting or having hosted ARTEX panels, with 1,608 live and publicly available instances at the time of the research. A metadata analysis of these servers gives valuable insights into the distribution and usage.

Additionally, 10 instances were misconfigured to expose the full ARTEX database – giving a rare insight into how actors prompted their agents, which models were used and the exact steps and attacks the agents carried out.

By Graciela Martínez
Tuesday, November 05, 2026
Cybersecurity challenges do not stop at national borders. Neither should our efforts to address them.
Strengthening incident response capabilities requires more than technology and technical expertise. It requires people, collaboration, trust, knowledge sharing and opportunities for teams to learn from one another.
These were some of the ideas behind the FIRST Regional Symposium for Latin America and the Caribbean, held on October 21–22, 2026, in Mendoza, Argentina, bringing together professionals from across the region to exchange experiences and discuss the challenges facing today's incident response community.
For me, this event represented an important opportunity to continue advancing a goal that has been central to my work at LACNIC CSIRT for many years: helping strengthen the capabilities of incident response teams and fostering a more connected and collaborative cybersecurity ecosystem in Latin America and the Caribbean.
Connecting a diverse regional community
The Symposium brought together professionals with different backgrounds and responsibilities, including CSIRT and SOC managers, cybersecurity analysts, network and infrastructure specialists, technical leaders, government representatives, law enforcement professionals and other stakeholders.
The attendee records included almost a hundred entries representing 17 countries, reflecting the regional and multidisciplinary nature of the community.
This diversity matters. Incident response is not the responsibility of a single type of organization. Effective cybersecurity requires cooperation among network operators, security teams, academia, public institutions, law enforcement and the wider Internet community.
Creating spaces where these different perspectives can meet, share experiences and establish professional connections is an essential part of building regional capacity.
From technical challenges to practical solutions
The technical program reflected the diversity and evolution of the challenges facing incident response teams.
Presentations addressed topics such as:

Large-scale network scanning and the transformation of technical findings into actionable threat intelligence.
Observability and cybersecurity monitoring in critical government infrastructure.
The use of multi-agent artificial intelligence to support incident prioritization, analysis and coordination.
Threat intelligence methodologies for identifying exposed infrastructure associated with Tor hidden services.
Lessons learned from developing a university CSIRT.
Email authentication standards, including SPF, DKIM and DMARC, as mechanisms to mitigate phishing and impersonation.
Systemic risks associated with technological monocultures in SOC and CSIRT environments.
Fundamental incident response practices and emerging warning signs for CSIRTs.

title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.
There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.
Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.
“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

title: The Shift: Rethinking the Human in the Loop
text:
PUBLISHED ON 05 NOV 2026

Megan Keeling, Insikt Group®

The Shift
A quarterly newsletter for security executives and cybersecurity leaders, offering thought leadership on the trends, risks, and strategic decisions redefining the security landscape.

Summary

Ensuring that there are "humans in the loop" is the gold safety standard for making sure artificial intelligence (AI) agentic systems act safely, ethically, and legally. However, as automated processes accelerate and scale, humans lose the ability to provide meaningful oversight over machine-speed workflows. Rather than simply inserting a human into a machine process, leaders must engineer systems that enable AI agents to operate at machine speed while ensuring they act within human-authorized intent, appropriate controls, and safety and legal boundaries. This means thinking strategically about where acceleration is possible and where slowing down to human speed is necessary to avoid catastrophic risk.

The Hiring Automation “Doom Loop” Is a WarningHiring offers an instructive example of how humans can be sidelined by a process accelerated by unchecked automation. Machine-assisted decision-making has long been used in the hiring process to manage volume and improve fairness and efficiency. However, generative AI has made reading and writing job applications almost completely machine-dominated, leading the CEO of Greenhouse, a human resources platform, to declare that AI had created a "doom loop" in hiring. No one intended to create this doom loop, but the adoption of automation in one area led to accelerated adoption in others, ultimately sidelining humans from hiring decisions.The hiring doom loop is driven by two mutually reinforcing trends: more applicants are applying for each position, and more companies are relying on automation to sift through the growing volume of applications. Applicants per hire tripled between 2021 and 2024, according to one survey of hiring managers, and Greenhouse reported a 412% increase in applicants per post. Applicants are almost certainly using generative AI to spin up customized applications to hundreds of jobs at once.Meanwhile, 91% of HR departments report using AI in recruitment, and Greenhouse data shows that the number of human recruiters has dropped by over 50%. The recruiters who remain cannot meaningfully evaluate any single application at this volume, further reducing human decision-making in the hiring process. Some companies now use AI to conduct interviews, meaning applicants may not meet an actual human at the company until very late in the process, if at all.Despite the intention of using AI to improve efficiency and manage scale, only one-third of recruiters reported improvements in time-to-hire using AI, while 25% reported it got slower. More companies are lengthening probationary periods, a sign that they're increasingly unable to identify unsuitable candidates before hiring them. Many job hunters express frustration with encountering bots instead of real humans at their potential future employer. At the same time, scammers and state-sponsored cybercriminals have taken advantage of this automated landscape to advance candidates whose real objective is to steal secrets or cryptocurrency.A few factors made hiring one of the first processes to fall victim to the doom loop. title: ThisBash Escape: Claude Dispatch Flaw Enables Browser Extensions RCE on the OS · Forever Security
text:
For security leaders
The context. Claude Dispatch lets people send work from their phone or browser to Claude Desktop, an AI agent that runs commands on their computer.
The problem. Any browser extension that can control claude.ai could use Dispatch to make Claude Desktop run code on the machine, even a different machine signed into the same Claude account.
Anthropic is retiring Dispatch, but not the design behind it. Other Claude features, like Claude Code Remote Control and Claude Cowork session, let the web drive an agent on the machine by design. Removing one feature does not address the issue fundamentally.
What it means for you. An employee signs into their personal Claude account on a work laptop. A malicious extension on their home browser now runs code on your corporate endpoint, next to your source code and cloud credentials.
The reason this matters. Connected AI assistants let low-privilege surfaces like the browser command high-privilege agents on the OS. With extensions on nearly every enterprise browser, governing extensions and AI agents is now part of endpoint security.

A malicious browser extension can read sensitive pages, steal information and act through your logged-in sessions. That is already a serious compromise. But permission to interact with a website should not give it permission to execute commands on your computer.
We found that Claude Dispatch could turn one into the other.
What begins with a browser extension installed on a personal computer may not end there. When AI assistants bridge personal and corporate environments, that seemingly minor compromise can become an initial access vector to organizational endpoints, where source code, cloud credentials, and other sensitive assets provide the next step toward an organization’s crown jewels.
Executive summary

Browser to OS. Claude Dispatch’s interface and API were reachable from an ordinary logged-in claude.ai session, so a browser extension able to control claude.ai could send commands to Claude Desktop as if they came from you.
No browser exploit needed. Four prompts and auto-clicked “Allow” buttons got Claude to install a package that opened Calculator. When Claude hesitated, prompt forcing supplied the reassurance in the user’s voice.
The impact ladder. On one machine, it is a sandbox escape. Across two machines, it is cross-machine RCE. Two machines plus a personal Claude account signed in on a work laptop, and it becomes organization infiltration.
Status. Reported to Anthropic on May 14, 2026, and acknowledged as valid. Anthropic says Dispatch will be retired, targeting the end of October 2026. Until then, this flaw remains exploitable.
The root cause goes beyond Dispatch. An authenticated web session is not, by itself, evidence that the user authorized a command on their machine. Yet that is the trust Claude’s connected architecture runs on, and it is shared by other features, such as Claude Code Remote Control and Claude Cowork session, which let the web drive a local agent by design.

Claude Dispatch lets users send instructions from another device to Claude Desktop, where an agent can work with local files and run commands. We discovered that its interface and API were also accessible through an ordinary authenticated session on claude.ai. An extension with permission to control that website could use this access to submit instructions to the desktop agent as though they came from the user.

Every honeypot vendor assumes attackers will eventually try to tell decoys from real systems. This is the first time we have recovered an autonomous attack agent's own plan for doing it, written down, sourced, tested and wired into the agent's decision loop. Below is the whole thing, layer by layer.

huntback's scanner fleet harvested the directory on 3 November 2026 between 21:08 and 21:13 UTC: 576 files across ports 8081 and 9001, with binaries on 8898. The listing root on 9001 is the system temp directory, which is what you get when someone runs python3 -m http.server from /tmp and forgets to stop it. ARTEX and the ARTEX-ymh fork
ARTEX is a multi-agent penetration testing system: a Go backend, a Next.js console, PostgreSQL, and an LLM planner that hands "intents" to LLM workers with shell access. It was published as open source in July 2026, has been widely reported in real intrusions this autumn, and was made closed-source by its developer in October; forks keep developing it. ARTEX-ymh is one of them. Its README describes the goal as "external breach, foothold, internal depth", and lists the honeypot module as subsystem seven of seven. Its documented test runs are against public training ranges, and nothing on this host shows activity against a real organisation.
The module is spread across the fork: a design document (HONEYPOT-DETECTION-DESIGN.md), the honeydetect signature package, agent hooks (agent/honeypot.go, agent/antitrap.go, agent/uapool.go, agent/untrusted.go), guard hooks (guard/egress.go, guard/tarpit.go), two database columns, and tests for each. The code refers to two delivery batches: "batch 5" for the agent's self-defences and "batch 6 L1" for static detection.

Executive summary
In 2025, several threat actors exploited CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771 (ToolShell vulnerabilities) in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint to achieve remote code execution through crafted HTTP requests. One of the threat actors deployed ransomware on the target’s systems after successful exploitation. Microsoft attributed this ransomware-related ToolShell activity to Storm-2603, distinguishing it from other actors whose observed activity was primarily focused on credential theft, espionage, and data exfiltration.
In December, our retrospective analysis identified activity consistent with Storm-2603’s TTPs. This activity involved the attacker using the IIS worker process as an in-memory bridge to the customer’s infrastructure, keeping the access and control layer entirely within w3wp.exe without writing anything to disk. Although subsequent post-exploitation activity generated disk artifacts, the bridge used to maintain access remained memory-resident.
Let’s look in more detail at this attack.
The attack chain, from reconnaissance to infrastructure compromise
Intrusion timeline: Strategic latency and exploitation
The intrusion analyzed in this report occurred in two stages, with a temporal gap between initial access and subsequent exploitation activity. The attack timeline was as follows:

Dec 20 – Vulnerability fingerprinting: A single HTTP request targeted a SharePoint administrative endpoint associated with the ToolPane component to determine whether the host was vulnerable to CVE-2025-53770.
Dec 21-23 – Tactical latency: A three-day period of silence followed the initial probe, separating the vulnerability fingerprinting from subsequent malicious activity and potentially reducing the likelihood of immediate detection.
Dec 24 – High-intensity re-engagement: On Christmas Eve, when security staffing at many companies is reduced, the full RCE chain was executed through the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) on the same endpoint as the initial probe.
Dec 26 – Incident discovery: The three-day gap initially prevented the December 20 probe from being correlated with subsequent malicious activity, marking the event as low priority. Retrospective analysis established that the probe was the initial phase of the subsequent intrusion.

A vulnerability fingerprinting request on December 20 marked the first observed interaction with the target. November 05, 2026
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Apple flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added an Apple flaw, tracked as CVE-2024-27834 (CVSS score of 5.5), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

“This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.” reads the advisory by CISA.

CVE-2024-27834 is a security vulnerability affecting Apple’s operating systems and Safari. It could allow an attacker who already has arbitrary read and write capabilities on a device to bypass Pointer Authentication (PAC), a hardware-based security mechanism designed to protect memory addresses and prevent certain types of memory-corruption attacks.

Pointer Authentication is a security feature implemented in Apple processors. It adds cryptographic signatures to pointers, helping ensure that memory addresses have not been maliciously modified.

An attacker who gains the ability to read and write arbitrary memory could potentially exploit CVE-2024-27834 to circumvent these protections. This could weaken an important security barrier and make further exploitation of the device easier.

What is the impact?

Bypassing Pointer Authentication protections.
Weakening defenses against memory-corruption attacks.
Potentially facilitating further exploitation when combined with other vulnerabilities.

Apple addressed the vulnerability through improved security checks in:

Safari 17.5
iOS 16.7.8 and iOS 17.5
iPadOS 16.7.8 and iPadOS 17.5
macOS Sonoma 14.5
tvOS 17.5

text: Key findingsAttackers using the Anubis ransomware targeted a U.S. organization in October 2026 using a new custom backdoor that Symantec has called Backdoor.Lindnor.The backdoor masqueraded as a Chrome component and as a VMware file, and was found on two Microsoft SQL Server machines.Within roughly an hour, the attackers dropped at least 13 executables to help terminate security services, along with five publicly known vulnerable drivers.The attackers also installed the legitimate remote access tool AnyDesk and a separate tool to run it in Safe Mode, likely to maintain access when security software was not fully running.The file encryption payload was blocked from execution, and there’s no evidence that any files were encrypted.Anubis has claimed approximately 96 victims in the past 12 months, and 52% of those victims are in the U.S.OverviewAttackers using the Anubis ransomware, which is developed by a group Symantec tracks as Hawkmoth, deployed a previously undocumented custom backdoor and an unusually large number of security software-disabling tools in an October 2026 attack on an organization in the U.S. Hawkmoth runs a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that emerged in December 2024 as a rebrand of the Sphinx ransomware. Its payload appears to be largely unchanged from the Sphinx version, with only the branding updated. In a July 2026 Anubis attack documented by Symantec, we noted that the threat actor used four different exfiltration tools (Megasync, WinSCP, Filezilla, S3browser) to steal data from the affected network and that it was unusual to see that many of the same type of tool deployed in a single attack. The group has claimed approximately 96 victims in the past 12 months, and the majority of them (52%) are located in the U.S., which aligns with previous targeting patterns by the group.We did not identify how the attackers gained initial access. text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

November 05, 2026
3 min read

Use LogPoint’s Search API, which works in two calls to the same endpoint, /getsearchlogs. The first call sends your query, time range and repos, and returns a search_id. The second call sends that search_id and returns the rows once the search is final. Both calls are form-encoded POSTs authenticated with your username and secret key.

LogPoint is a popular SIEM in Europe, and the Search API is the cleanest way to get a defined slice of its data out. Prime Core has 19,598 detection rules for LogPoint, mapped to 664 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get logs out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Your secret key. Every API call carries your LogPoint username and secret key. You find the key in your user profile’s access key settings. Treat it like a password.

Repo names. Searches run against repos, written as <ip>:5504/<repo>, for example 127.0.0.1:5504/_logpoint. The same endpoint family lists them for you (getalloweddata with type logpoint_repos).

Time range. time_range takes either a preset like “Last 24 hours” or a pair of epoch seconds. For incident work, use the epoch pair; date -d ‘2026-10-19T00:00:00Z’ +%s computes it.

Export with the Search API

LP="https://logpoint.example.com"# 1. start the search (2026-10-19 00:00 UTC to 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC)SID=$(curl -sS "$LP/getsearchlogs" \  --data-urlencode "username=$LP_USER" --data-urlencode "secret_key=$LP_KEY" \  --data-urlencode 'requestData={"query": "device_ip=10.0.0.5", "time_range": [1792368000, 1792454400], "limit": 10000, "repos": ["127.0.0.1:5504/_logpoint"]}' \  | jq -r '.search_id')# 2. fetch results until the search is finalwhile :; do  R=$(curl -sS "$LP/getsearchlogs" \      --data-urlencode "username=$LP_USER" --data-urlencode "secret_key=$LP_KEY" \      --data-urlencode "requestData={\"search_id\": \"$SID\"}")  [ "$(echo "$R" | jq -r '.final')" = "true" ] && break  sleep 3doneecho "$R" | jq -c '.rows[]' > logpoint_1019.jsonlecho "$R" | jq -r '.rows[].msg // empty' > logpoint_1019_raw.log

Keep the query a filter. A query with | chart or other aggregations returns aggregated rows, not logs. The raw log usually sits in the msg field.

Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file.

Sanitize.

Review.

When it goes wrong

SymptomLikely causeFixAuthentication errorWrong username or secret keyCopy the key again from your profileEmpty resultsWrong repo string, or the time range is in millisecondsList repos via getalloweddata; use epoch secondsAggregated rows instead of logsQuery includes chart or similarUse a plain filterResults cut shortlimit reachedRaise it, or split the windowRequest rejectedNot sent as form dataSend application/x-www-form-urlencoded

Before you start

Access to Investigate. You need a role that can investigate the service (Broker or Concentrator) holding the logs.

Set the export format once. In Profile → Preferences → Investigation, the Export Log Format preference decides the default format for downloads: Text, XML, CSV or JSON. Choose Text for raw logs. If it’s left empty, NetWitness asks every time.

Use the Devo Query API: send a LINQ query, a time range and an output mode to the /search/query endpoint of your region, authenticated with an API token or key and secret. Ask for a JSON mode and you get structured events; select the message field from raw tables to get the original lines back. The official Python SDK (devo-sdk) wraps the same API if you prefer code to curl.

Devo stores large volumes of security and operational data in the cloud, often with long retention. Prime Core has 23,653 detection rules for Devo, mapped to 664 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Credentials. Create an API token, or an API key and secret, in your Devo domain’s credentials settings, with access to the tables you need.

Your region’s endpoint. The Query API host depends on where your domain lives, for example apiv2-us.devo.com or apiv2-eu.devo.com.

Table names. Devo organizes data in tables like box.unix or firewall.fortinet.traffic. Find yours in the Data Search area, and build the query there first.

curl -sS -X POST "https://apiv2-eu.devo.com/search/query" \  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVO_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \  -d '{    "query": "from box.unix where hostname = \"web-03\" select eventdate, hostname, message",    "from": 1792368000,    "to": 1792454400,    "mode": {"type": "json/simple"}  }' > devo_web03_1019.json

The from and to values above are epoch seconds for 2026-10-19 00:00 UTC to 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC. If the response is one JSON object per line, upload it as-is. If it’s an array, flatten it with jq -c ‘.[]’. For raw lines, extract message.

Python alternative. pip install devo-sdk, then use the API client from the devo.api package with your token, the same query and dates. It handles the request signing for key-and-secret authentication.

title: CVE-2026-109518: APT Flaw Enables MitM Root Code Execution
text:
A high-severity vulnerability in APT, the package management system used by Debian, Ubuntu, and derivative Linux distributions, could allow an on-path attacker to replace a verified software package with a malicious one and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-109518, the flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 7.7 and affects APT’s HTTP download and retry handling.

The vulnerability is caused by improper handling of hard links when APT follows HTTP redirects and retries failed package downloads. Under the right conditions, two different downloads can be merged after a redirect causes them to resolve to the same URI. An attacker able to manipulate traffic between an APT client and a repository can abuse this behavior to substitute an attacker-controlled .deb package after verification has already taken place.

Because Debian packages can execute installation scripts with root privileges, successful exploitation can result in complete system compromise. However, exploitation requires several conditions: the victim must initiate a package installation, APT must communicate over manipulable HTTP, and the Acquire::Retries option must be set to a non-zero value.

Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and newer releases are exposed by default because retries are enabled. Debian has similarly enabled retries by default since APT 2.3.2, including Debian 12. Older releases can still be vulnerable when administrators or automation scripts manually enable retries.

Contact Sales

The vulnerability was discovered by security researcher Max Justicz and publicly disclosed on November 4, 2026. Debian and Ubuntu released security updates on the same day. Neither vendor advisory currently reports exploitation of the flaw in real-world attacks.

CVE-2026-109518 analysis

CVE-2026-109518 affects APT deployments on Debian, Ubuntu, and derivative Linux distributions when package files are downloaded over an attacker-manipulable HTTP path and retry functionality is enabled. Ubuntu classifies the vulnerability as High with a CVSS 4.0 score of 7.7 and the vector CVSS:4.0/AV/AC/AT/PR/UI/VC/VI/VA/SC/SI/SA.

APT is responsible for downloading, verifying, and installing packages on Debian-based Linux systems. Package authenticity normally relies on Debian and Ubuntu repository signature mechanisms designed to ensure that packages delivered by mirrors cannot be silently modified by an untrusted intermediary.

CVE-2026-109518 breaks an important part of this trust model under specific download conditions.

The vulnerability occurs when APT handles HTTP redirects and retries. According to Debian’s advisory, APT can merge two separate package downloads when a redirect causes them to share the same URI. When a download subsequently needs to be resumed, incorrect handling of reused hard links can allow the content associated with an already verified package to be overwritten.

An attacker first needs the ability to manipulate HTTP traffic between the victim and the package archive. title: CVE-2026-98432: Critical Linux Kernel TCP Flaw Enables Remote Code Execution
text:
En

CVEs

November 05, 2026
10 min read

A critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel’s IPv4 TCP networking stack could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to trigger memory corruption, crash vulnerable systems, and potentially execute arbitrary code with root privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-98432, the flaw carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 and has existed in the Linux kernel since version 4.4.

The vulnerability stems from a race condition that can cause the kernel to access IP option data after the underlying memory has already been freed. An attacker capable of reaching an exposed IPv4 TCP service can attempt to trigger the condition using specially timed connection requests containing IPv4 options. No authentication, local privileges, or user interaction are required.

Security interest increased significantly after Anthropic disclosed that an internal Claude research model had developed a working exploit capable of achieving remote root command execution against a Linux server with a Multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener. The exploit first leaks a kernel pointer to bypass KASLR and then uses the same use-after-free condition to corrupt memory and redirect kernel control flow. Anthropic has not released the exploit code.

Importantly, the underlying vulnerability is not limited to MPTCP. Red Hat confirms that systems with ordinary IPv4 TCP networking remain vulnerable even when MPTCP is disabled, including default Red Hat Enterprise Linux configurations.

Contact Sales

As of November 4, 2026, no Linux vendor, CERT, or other reviewed source has reported confirmed exploitation of the flaw in real-world attacks. Public research code demonstrating portions of the vulnerability exists, but a publicly released exploit providing the full remote-root capability demonstrated by Anthropic has not been documented.

Security teams can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to strengthen their defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation, operationalize threat intelligence, and accelerate threat hunting across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Detect CVE-2026-98432 by monitoring unusual IPv4 TCP traffic containing IP options, repeated connection attempts designed to trigger race conditions, kernel crashes or memory-corruption events, and suspicious activity that could indicate successful post-exploitation.

Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added.

CVE-2026-98432 analysis

CVE-2026-98432 affects the IPv4 TCP connection-handling code in Linux kernels containing the vulnerable implementation introduced in Linux 4.4. The Linux kernel CVE team classifies the issue as critical with a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 and the vector AV/AC/PR/UI/S/C/I/A.

The vulnerability is a use-after-free condition caused by a race during concurrent TCP connection processing. When an IPv4 TCP connection is established, tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers IP options associated with the pending request to the newly created socket without making a separate copy.

Another CPU can simultaneously process a retransmitted SYN associated with the same request socket. During that process, functions responsible for generating the SYN-ACK continue reading the IP options while protected by an RCU read-side critical section.

However, the child socket can be destroyed while that operation is still underway. The kernel then frees the associated inet_opt structure using kfree(), leaving another CPU potentially accessing memory that has already been released. The resulting stale reference creates a use-after-free condition in ip_options_build().

Image: Shutterstock

Devices on the White House network are being used as proxies allowing outside users to appear as if they come from the president's office, researchers found.See Also: OnDemand | Zero Trust in Action: The New Rules of Federal Data Protection

Security firm Layer3 Intel stumbled on the White House network while probing services that sell access to everyday devices for traffic reroute. It found that 28 residential proxy services provided access to the Washington network.

Between Oct. 5 and Nov. 3, those providers routed researchers' internet traffic through six White House IP addresses hundreds of times.

"We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it," Layer3 Intel said Wednesday in a blog. "We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services."

Traffic from the White House devices showed up between 5 p.m. and midnight and almost none in the early morning. The pattern suggests that it came from a person powering on the devices and regularly working late rather than a public guest Wi-Fi, Layer3 Intel said.

Residential proxy detection service Synthient also observed the pattern on the same White House IP addresses. It found several staffers were running Windows 11 machines infected with a proxy Software Development Kit called Infatica SDK. The White House didn't respond to a request for comment.

"Infatica's founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia's state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016," security blogger Brian Krebs wrote.

Fomenko advertised on LinkedIn that his company has expanded from selling IP addresses at scale to giving customers "clean, structured data" from the websites they need, "without spending engineering cycles fighting anti-bot systems like Cloudflare and Akamai."

Infatica was one of many White House IP resellers. These residential proxy services are publicly available. Anyone could rent someone else's internet address through these providers with a few dollars and anonymize their web traffic, Layer3 Intel said.

Residential proxies can expose internal networks to hackers, allowing them to move laterally and spread malware to additional devices, Layer3 Intel said.

Previous research by Synthient found Kimwolf, the Android variant of the Aisuru DDoS Botnet, propagated to at least 2 million compromised devices by exploiting proxy networks.

Unsecured proxy SDKs could allow access to the public internet but also to private IP addresses accessible from the device. Attackers could probe the device's local network for vulnerable systems, send infection requests through the residential proxy infrastructure and cause those systems to install malicious payloads.

If an SDK on the White House network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems, Layer3 Intel said.

IP security firm Spur also confirmed proxy activity on the White House network, Layer3 Intel said. The firm's January research identified residential proxies in nearly 300 government-owned networks spanning large blocks of IP addresses.

text: Cyber Security News Ubuntu Releases Security Fixes for Critical Linux Kernel Vulnerability Allowing Remote Code Execution Ubuntu has made fixes available for CVE-2026-98432, a critical Linux kernel vulnerability allowing remote code execution through IPv4 TCP connection handling. The flaw carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, while Ubuntu assigns it High priority. Fixes for Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and newer are undergoing qualification in the -proposed pocket. The patching push now coincides with suspected malicious reconnaissance. Security researcher Marcus Hutchins, known as MalwareTech, reports internet-wide MPTCP scanning and more than two million reachable endpoints, although these are not confirmed vulnerable systems. Suspected Attackers Probe Port 443 In an update, Hutchins said residential proxies and Russian-based VPN servers were observed scanning port 443 using MPTCP-enabled connections as of November 2. The connections transmitted no HTTP data, suggesting targeted vulnerability discovery rather than ordinary web indexing. Hutchins suspects threat actor involvement, but the observations do not establish attribution or successful exploitation. He reported no known public RCE exploit, although denial-of-service proofs of concept are circulating. Developing reliable RCE reportedly remains difficult, potentially favoring well-resourced attackers. An October 30 scan identified approximately 2,102,043 servers accepting MPTCP connections on port 443. A deeper scan completing TLS negotiation returned approximately 762,774 systems. Neither measurement establishes whether endpoints run unpatched kernels. Hutchins argues that exposure could be closer to the larger figure because exploitation does not require a valid HTTP connection. These measurements describe reachable infrastructure, not a verified count of exploitable machines. He also reports that several kernels, including Debian’s, enable MPTCP by default, and that Go 1.24+ applications can create MPTCP listeners when kernel support is enabled, citing Caddy as an example. Kernel Flaw and Patch Availability The vulnerability involves unsafe ownership of IPv4 options during TCP connection setup. Concurrent processing can access options after their memory is freed, producing a use-after-free. The fix defers freeing through kfree_rcu(). Such lifetime errors also underpin the separate SCTPhantom networking vulnerability and Linux bridge STP flaw, illustrating recurring kernel memory-safety challenges. Ubuntu’s supplied release notice identifies proposed builds 5.15.0-203.213 for 22.04, 6.8.0-149.149 for 24.04, and 7.0.0-43.43 for 26.04. It lists 26.10 as fixed in 7.3.0-10.10, but the public tracker still labels that build work in progress. Administrators should verify package-specific status before deployment. Administrators can inspect listeners with sudo ss -Mlnp. Hutchins warns that setting net.mptcp.enabled=0 does not close existing sockets; affected applications must restart to remove those listeners. However, MPTCP is not the underlying vulnerability boundary. Ubuntu’s technical description concerns IPv4 options handling, and its packet-filtering workaround explicitly reduces risk without fully preventing exploitation. Kernel updates remain essential. Following the disclosure of critical Linux kernel networking exposure, administrators should inventory internet-facing services, validate proposed kernels through acceptance testing, install the appropriate fixed packages, and reboot before considering remediation complete. The Capital One Ventures-led Series C funding will help New York-based Sentra build data loss protection into a broader data security platform, develop AI governance and agentic AI capabilities, strengthen identity and access controls, and continue to invest in core data discovery and classification, said co-founder and CEO Yoav Regev. He said the money will support product development as organizations adopt AI.
"What we could see in the last two years is that AI is a data problem, and there is no way to solve those problems that are coming with AI without the data," Regev told ISMG. "The agentic era has just started, and we are going to see it exploding in the next few years."
Sentra, founded in 2021, employs 210 people and has raised $253 million in four rounds of outside funding, with Key1 Capital leading the firm's $50 million Series B funding round in April 2025. The company has been led since its its inception by Regev, who spent nearly 24 years in Israel's Unit 8200, culminating in a stint as the head of its cyber department (see: Startup Sentra Nabs $50M to Boost AI-Powered Data Protection).
Helping Organizations Prepare for AI Adoption
Customers increasingly want an end-to-end data security platform rather than isolated capabilities, and Regev sees DLP, DSPM, AI security and identity as connected parts of that platform. DLP decisions are more effective when informed by data context such as what the data is, where it resides and who can access it, rather than being made without that context at endpoints or in email, Regev said.
"Organizations need a full data security platform end to end," Regev said. "You cannot find such a solution these days. DLP is one aspect, the infrastructure that we have today is one aspect, and AI security and the combination between identities and data is one of the most important parts today to solve the agentic problem."
Regev believes Sentra's investments in identity will provide an access intelligence layer that maps people and non-human identities - including agents - and connects those identities to data. This could support adaptive, time-limited permissions, so agents receive only the access needed for a particular task, Regev said.
"We are going to connect the dots between the identities, mainly the non-human identities, such as the agents and the data," Regev said. "With that, you can ensure adaptive permissions because you cannot follow the agents, so you need those identities to get on-demand permissions and on-demand access to the data."
Sentra currently helps organizations prepare for AI adoption by identifying sensitive data and reducing the risk that it is exposed to the wrong models or surfaced to unauthorized users through tools such as copilots, Regev said. Current use cases for Sentra include data hygiene, AI readiness and addressing excessive permissions in AI workflows, Regev said.
"You don't want to take your sensitive data and push it to the models," Regev said. "On the other hand, you don't want your Copilot or Gemini, or whichever solution you have, to retrieve the wrong data to the wrong person."

title: GitHub to Block pull_request_target Workflows by Default Starting December 2
text: BackSecurity NewsGitHub to Block pull_request_target Workflows by Default Starting December 2GitHub is tightening GitHub Actions security with new restrictions on privileged pull request workflows. Here's what changes and how maintainers are affected.Sarah GoodingNov 5, 2026|4 min read GitHub will begin blocking GitHub Actions workflows triggered by pull_request_target in public repositories on December 2, 2026, expanding its protections against a class of CI/CD vulnerabilities that has repeatedly enabled attackers to steal credentials and compromise open source software releases.The restriction, originally announced in September, will prevent affected workflows from running unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. GitHub had initially scheduled enforcement for November 2 but confirmed the postponed December 2 deadline in a new update this week, giving maintainers additional time to review their automation and configure exceptions.The new restriction goes beyond protections introduced in June, when GitHub updated actions/checkout to prevent common attempts to check out untrusted pull request code inside privileged workflows. This time, GitHub is blocking the pull_request_target trigger itself by default, including for workflows that use it safely. GitHub introduced pull_request_target in 2020 to help maintainers automate tasks involving pull requests from external contributors. Unlike the standard pull_request event, which restricts access to secrets and provides a read-only token for contributions from forks, pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository with access to its configured secrets and token permissions.That elevated access makes the trigger useful for legitimate maintenance tasks such as assigning reviewers, labeling pull requests, and posting authenticated comments. The workflow definition runs from the repository's trusted default branch, rather than the contributor's proposed changes.The security risk emerges when that privileged workflow checks out and executes code from an untrusted fork or passes attacker-controlled pull request data into shell commands. A malicious contributor can exploit those mistakes to execute commands with access to credentials and other resources intended only for trusted automation.Researchers have warned about these vulnerabilities, commonly called "pwn requests," since at least 2021. Variations of this attack pattern contributed to major supply chain incidents involving Nx, PostHog, and TanStack.GitHub's June changes addressed a common source of these vulnerabilities by making actions/checkout reject unsafe fork checkouts in privileged workflows unless explicitly overridden. The December policy takes a broader approach, preventing the event from triggering a workflow at all unless administrators have authorized it through an applicable policy. GitHub's default restriction currently operates in evaluation mode, allowing affected workflows to continue running before enforcement begins.The company has scheduled two temporary enforcement periods, known as brownouts, to expose configurations that will stop working under the new policy:November 9, 16:00–18:00 UTCNovember 16, 16:00–18:00 UTCDuring those windows, blocked pull_request_target attempts will generate failed workflow runs with an error annotation instead of executing. title: Ninth Circuit: Breach Of Confidence Confers Standing In Health Data Security Case
text:
Claire E. Castles, Amanda Fitzsimmons, Nathaniel P. Garrett, Rebekah Byers Kcehowski, Mary Alexander Myers, and Alexander H. Southwell of Jones Day write:
Departing from the risk-based approach many courts have applied since TransUnion, and in tension with other circuits, the Ninth Circuit held that health plan participants whose confidential health information was disclosed without authorization suffered a concrete injury, even absent financial loss or a risk of future harm.
Background
On October 9, 2026, the Ninth Circuit revived a putative class action in Black v. IEC Group, Inc., holding that health plan participants whose confidential information was disclosed without authorization have standing to sue in federal court. An employee of the plan’s administrator had mistakenly emailed a spreadsheet of participants’ claims information to other plan members. The spreadsheet listed participants’ names, provider names, claim numbers, dates of service, and amounts billed or paid. The district court dismissed the case because the plaintiffs could not show a substantial likelihood of future harm, such as identity theft.
The Court’s Analysis
The Ninth Circuit took a different view. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, an intangible harm supports standing if it closely resembles a harm courts have traditionally recognized. The court found that analogue in the centuries-old action for breach of confidence, explaining that “a trust betrayed is the harm.” It emphasized the administrator’s promises, including in its privacy policy, to keep the information confidential and noted that breach of contract claims have long been actionable without financial loss. The court also cited HIPAA as evidence that Congress views such information as worth protecting, even though the statute does not allow private suits. Because every claim rested on the same disclosure, the court resolved standing for all of them at once.
