Leak Site Screenshot Screenshot captured at time of discovery. Image blurred to protect victim PII. × Claim Summary
On or around November 4, 2026, a ransomware group calling itself Whitearmor allegedly posted Unilever to its dark web leak site. Unilever is a British multinational consumer goods company headquartered in London, with a portfolio of more than 400 brands including Dove, Knorr, Hellmann’s, and Rexona, operating across beauty, personal care, home care, and foods in roughly 190 countries.
According to the threat actor, the group claims to hold a substantial trove of internal records, including what it describes as 665K contacts, 5.5K “OTM” accounts with roles and logins, 14M locations, 3.8M shipments, 229M status records, 13.8K invoices, and 838K distributor loyalty profiles and ledgers. Whitearmor purports that the total dataset is approximately 79 gigabytes across 1.8 million files spanning three regions.
The group further claims a ransom demand of $15,000,000 in Bitcoin. None of these figures have been independently confirmed, and the underlying data has not been verified by Yazoul Security or any third party.
Threat Actor Profile
Whitearmor is a relatively low-profile ransomware operation with no established public research footprint at the time of writing. Yazoul Security has no confirmed victim count, no documented tooling, and no published YARA rules or detection signatures attributable to this group. This absence of a track record is itself a significant credibility caveat.
Because the group’s known tools and tactics are undocumented, defenders should not assume any specific initial access vector, encryption routine, or exfiltration method. The claim references “OTM accounts with roles and logins,” which, if genuine, would suggest access to identity or operational management systems, but this remains unverified. Organizations should treat the group as an unknown quantity and apply general ransomware resilience controls rather than signature-specific defenses. No detection guidance is currently available from public sources.
Alleged Data Exposure
The actor’s description of the data is unusually broad for a manufacturing-sector victim, spanning contact records, shipment and logistics data, invoice records, and distributor loyalty ledgers. If accurate, such a combination could include business contact information, operational logistics details, and commercial relationship data.
Yazoul Security has not seen, reviewed, or validated any of the claimed data. We do not publish samples, download links, credentials, or access instructions, and none are included here. The claimed volume of 79GB and 1.8 million files is asserted solely by the threat actor and should be treated with skepticism. Ransomware groups frequently inflate data volumes and record counts to increase pressure on victims.
Potential Impact
If the claim is genuine, potential impacts could include exposure of business contact and commercial relationship data, disruption or embarrassment tied to logistics and shipment records, and reputational risk for a consumer-facing brand portfolio. Supply chain partners and distributors could face secondary risk if loyalty and ledger data were exposed.
However, these are hypothetical scenarios based on unverified actor claims. There is no confirmation of data authenticity, exfiltration, encryption, or operational disruption. A $15M demand against an organization of Unilever’s scale is notably low relative to typical enterprise extortion figures, which may indicate either an opportunistic operation or an attempt to pressure a quick settlement.

"At this time, we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated," Chainalysis told customers.

Chainalysis: exposed credentials, live tokens, and personal data
Chainalysis confirmed Wednesday evening that the intrusion detected on October 30 included access to usernames, password hashes, and live tokens. The company had earlier disclosed that user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels were exposed. Chainalysis said it has not confirmed the type of hashing algorithm used to protect passwords, a detail that limits public assessment of how vulnerable those hashes are to offline cracking.
Some users received emails instructing them to change passwords, but Chainalysis also said the password-reset functionality is currently down. The company advised users to change passwords on other sites where they reuse credentials.

Services taken offline: Reactor, Data Solutions, KYT, and access controls
Chainalysis detected "abnormal activity" on its transaction screening products and has taken multiple services offline while its teams work. Affected services include the Reactor blockchain investigation platform used by international law enforcement customers, the Data Solutions threat intelligence platform, and the KYT (know your transaction) anti-money laundering solution's user interface and login page.
The company said it plans to reinstate KYT and the risk-intelligence Address Screening tool "at some point today (Thursday November 5)." When restoring access, Chainalysis will require customers to provide trusted IP addresses to the company’s support team or their account manager so they can be added to an allowlist; only after that will users be able to begin resetting passwords. Chainalysis also said it will require "every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate."

Chainalysis has not publicly named an attacker, but implied the culprits used an AI agent and likened the intrusion to attacks that have hit "many other tech platforms in recent weeks." The company said its teams are working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden systems.

Chainalysis reiterated it had "no evidence" that investigations data or attribution information were accessed or altered. November 5, 2026

Posted by

Image: @depositphotos

Journalists in Uzbekistan found their own personal information and details about relatives in a database circulating online, Gazeta.uz has reported. The Interior Ministry announced an investigation on October 29 after reports linked the records to SAFE Service, formerly known as SafeRoad, a digital service for motorists. As of November 5, the authorities had yet to announce their findings.
Separately, on November 1, a hacker group known as Butterfly claimed it had accessed a government database containing personal information on more than 27 million Uzbek citizens. The group said it had accessed passport details, addresses, phone numbers, personal identification numbers (PINFL), and biometric photographs belonging to millions of people.
To support its claims, the group published Digital Technologies Minister Sherzod Shermatov’s phone number and threatened to sell the database on the dark web, a part of the internet accessible through specialized software that is also used to trade stolen data.
By November 3, Butterfly had recast itself as a community of “white-hat hackers,” cybersecurity specialists who identify vulnerabilities in computer systems so they can be fixed. The group’s members said they had not stolen government databases and had instead sought to highlight security weaknesses and the slow response of the agencies responsible. The group did not explain why it had initially threatened to sell the alleged database. It is also unclear whether Butterfly’s members had permission from the owners of the information systems, as is customary in authorized security testing.
Shermatov commented on the situation on November 4. Without confirming reports of a data breach, the minister warned about vulnerabilities in outdated information systems. He said artificial intelligence was making software vulnerabilities easier to discover and urged government agencies and businesses to conduct more frequent security checks and heed warnings from UzCERT, Uzbekistan’s national computer incident response service. He did not say whether the authorities had verified Butterfly’s claims or established the origin of the alleged data.
The Interior Ministry and the Cybersecurity Center under the State Security Service are investigating the origin of the records linked in October reports to SAFE Service. The developer, AUTODOC, denied that the records came from its application, saying the information had been collected from other sources before the application was launched.
No connection between the two incidents has been established. Butterfly’s withdrawal of its initial claim and AUTODOC’s explanation do not establish where the published information originated.
Cybersecurity specialist Akmal Sodikov notes that personal data can become accessible to unauthorized parties because of server misconfigurations, inadequate access controls, employee actions, or vulnerabilities in third-party services. Passport details, phone numbers, and PINFL numbers are valuable to fraudsters. With such information, criminals can more easily impersonate bank employees or government officials to trick people into disclosing verification codes and gain access to their accounts.
In Uzbekistan, government services, digital identification, and financial transactions are becoming increasingly interconnected. As a result, protecting personal data depends on the security of multiple information systems.

# $6.3 Billion Binance Theft Triggers Fed and OCC Cybersecurity Probes

6.3 billion.

That is the number dominating every screen in the financial sector this afternoon. It's a figure so large it ceases to be a theft and becomes a macroeconomic event. While most of the wire is treating the Binance hack as a tragedy of lost digits, the more interesting story is the reaction from the Federal Reserve and the OCC. They aren't worried about the missing crypto; they're worried about contagion.

When the Fed starts probing bank cybersecurity because of a breach at a third-party exchange, we've moved past a simple security failure. This is a second-order effect where the fragility of one entity threatens the stability of the broader financial plumbing. The regulators have realized that Wall Street's connectivity to these platforms creates a bridge for systemic risk.

It’s an expensive lesson in trust, though not the most expensive one on my desk today. Crédit Mutuel Arkéa just confirmed a supply chain attack via a service provider that cost them roughly $133 million. The loss is smaller than the Binance figure, but the mechanism—a compromised provider—is far more common and harder to defend against.

I have a low tolerance for the word "critical" in advisories. Usually, it's used by vendors to induce panic or by researchers to get a headline. But when $6.3 billion vanishes or a bank loses $133 million due to a vendor's failure, the label is earned.

The noise this week has been deafening. There were 473 stories on data breaches alone. Most of them are filler. The real signal is usually found in the boring lists, like CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

On November 4, CISA added CVE-2024-27834 to the list. It's an improper authentication vulnerability affecting multiple Apple products. The federal patch deadline is November 18. That gives agencies exactly two weeks to secure their devices before they are officially considered negligent.

The irony is that attackers are already using this patched flaw to deliver info-stealing malware. This is where the argument for "critical" usually falls apart in the real world. A vulnerability isn't critical because it *could* be exploited; it's critical when it *is* being exploited and people still aren't patching. The gap between a patch release and its actual deployment on an endpoint is the only metric that actually matters.

Some will argue that the Binance heist is an outlier, a "black swan" event caused by unique architectural flaws in cryptocurrency exchanges. They’ll say it has nothing to do with the day-to-day grind of patching Apple devices or monitoring supply chain providers.

They're wrong. The common thread isn't the technology; it's the persistence of an assumed security posture. Whether it's a crypto exchange believing its hot wallets are isolated or a bank believing its service provider is secure, the failure is always the same: trusting a perimeter that doesn't actually exist.

The Binance hack rhymes with the 2014 Mt. Gox collapse in scale, but the parallel breaks down at the regulatory level. In 2014, the regulators were mostly confused by what a blockchain was. Now, they are terrified of how it’s integrated into the global ledger. The fear has shifted from "what is this?" to "how do we stop this from taking down the banks?"

If I see the Fed issue a formal directive on liquidity requirements for firms interacting with digital asset providers, I'll know that 6.3 billion was the tipping point. Until then, it's just another very large number in a week full of them.

I suspect we'll see more "contagion" probes before the month is out. The question is whether those probes will actually result in better architecture or just more paperwork for the people who are already struggling to hit their November 18 deadline.

Claim Summary
On or around November 3, 2026, the ransomware group tracked as incransom allegedly added fidepartners.com, a Spain-based organization operating in the financial services sector, to its dark web leak site. According to the threat actor, the listing identifies the victim by domain and country (ES) and categorizes the target as financial services. The group has purportedly not disclosed the volume of data it claims to hold, and the “claimed data” field in the leak site entry appears empty or unspecified.
At this time, there is no public confirmation from Fide Partners that any security incident has occurred. The claim remains unverified and should be treated as an assertion by the threat actor rather than an established fact. Ransomware operators frequently post victim names before negotiations conclude, and some listings are later removed, retracted, or shown to be exaggerated. Readers should not assume that data was exfiltrated or that operations were disrupted based solely on this listing.
Threat Actor Profile
The group behind this claim is incransom, sometimes referred to as INC Ransom. Public tracking of this group remains limited. According to available intelligence, the total number of known victims is unknown, and there is no confirmed public research detailing the group’s specific toolset or tactics. The leak site entry itself provides no technical indicators, no sample files, and no stated data volume.
Because the group’s known tools are undocumented in our current dataset, we cannot attribute specific malware families, initial access vectors, or exfiltration methods to this claim. Analysts should avoid assuming a particular playbook. Where detection guidance or YARA rules become available for this actor, they should be validated against current telemetry before deployment. Absent verified indicators, defenders should rely on general ransomware resilience controls rather than actor-specific signatures.
Alleged Data Exposure
The threat actor claims to have targeted a financial services firm in Spain. However, the claimed data volume is undisclosed, and no data samples, file listings, or proof-of-compromise artifacts have been publicly described in the information available to us. This is a significant gap: many ransomware groups publish sample files or directory trees to pressure victims, and the absence of such detail may indicate an early-stage claim, an unverified assertion, or a listing that has not yet been substantiated.
We are not reproducing any leaked content, credentials, or access details, and none have been confirmed. The nature and scope of any allegedly exposed information remain unknown.
Potential Impact
If the claim is accurate, a financial services organization could face risks including operational disruption, regulatory scrutiny under Spanish and EU data protection frameworks, and reputational harm. Financial sector victims are attractive targets because of regulatory pressure to restore services quickly. However, these are potential consequences only. No breach, data loss, or service interruption has been confirmed.
What to Watch For

Official statements from Fide Partners or its representatives confirming or denying an incident.
Regulatory notifications, if any, from Spanish or EU authorities.
Removal or modification of the leak site listing, which can indicate negotiation or retraction.
Emergence of verified technical indicators tied to this actor. Monitor our intel and advisory pages for updates.

title: Aérospatial et Défense : Quand la maîtrise de l’information devient une arme de souveraineté
text:
Aérospatial et Défense : Quand la maîtrise de l’information devient une arme de souveraineté

Alexandra Vilar

Publié le
05/11/2026

Crédit : 3AF (Association Aéronautique et Astronautique de France)

« Stocker l’information, c’est la contrôler. » Dans une guerre où la compétition se joue dans l’espace, la gestion des données devient le nouveau champ de bataille des grandes puissances. Contrôler l’information est aujourd’hui essentiel pour protéger la souveraineté.

Face à ces enjeux, la 3AF (Association Aéronautique et Astronautique de France) annonce la tenue de son 18ème Forum Européen d’intelligence Économique et Stratégique (IES). Ce colloque, soutenu par le Portail de l’IE en tant que partenaire média, s’annonce comme le point d’orgue d’une rencontre riche en échanges avec des experts de la défense, de l’aéronautique et du spatial. L’évènement se déroulera sur deux jours, les 25 et 26 novembre prochain, à Angoulême.

Société savante reconnue en France, la 3AF est la référence du secteur aérospatial. Fondée en 1972 et reconnue d’utilité publique, elle rassemble plus de 1500 experts : ingénieurs, chercheurs, décideurs politiques et industriels de premier plan comme Airbus, Safran et le Centre national d’études spatiales(CNES). Acteur clé, elle conjugue les savoirs afin de développer les innovations technologiques et de guider la transition écologique dans le secteur. À travers ses commissions techniques, la 3AF, outre sa qualité de visionnaire sur l’avenir du vol et de la propulsion, anticipe les menaces technologiques et opérationnelles qui pèsent sur l’aérospatial français et européen.

À l’aune des cyberattaques ciblant les infrastructures spatiales et militaires, dont le volet numérique constitue l’un des piliers de la guerre hybride, la 3AF porte une vision moderne de l’Intelligence Économique et Stratégique (IES) : l’enjeu n’est plus tant de construire des vecteurs souverains, mais de sanctuariser l’ensemble de l’écosystème industriel et des données pour garantir notre sécurité nationale et européenne. En appréhendant l’information brute comme une matière première critique, la démarche de la 3AF et des experts en IES dépasse la simple logique de stockage de l’information. Il s’agit désormais de sécuriser le patrimoine informationnel tout en convertissant cette donnée brute en un véritable avantage décisionnel.

Cette année, cette dynamique est au cœur des débats du 18ème Forum de l’IES. Placé sous le thème de « L’intelligence économique face aux affrontements géostratégiques », ce rendez-vous crucial met en exergue l’obligation pour les organisations d’« agir pour transformer l’information en avantage décisif » face à l’accélération des compétitions mondiales et aux ruptures technologiques contemporaines.

L’intérêt fondamental de ces deux journées réside dans la capacité des acteurs à redéfinir l’intelligence économique dans l’environnement géostratégique, et non plus à la voir comme un simple outil d’observation mais comme un véritable instrument de souveraineté et de résilience face aux dépendances critiques.

En sa qualité d’« éclaireur », l’expert en IES trouve dans ce forum l’opportunité de concrétiser une véritable approche stratégique. Grâce aux échanges et au partage de connaissances, l’objectif est de bâtir une action collective et décloisonnée. That is the right direction. Europe cannot wait for a single federal defence structure before acting.Europe’s defence capacity is inevitably fragmented. A military operation may depend on a French port, a German railway, a Polish electricity network, privately operated telecommunications and capabilities supplied by countries outside the EU.They do not need a common owner. But somebody must be responsible for whether the system works when it is needed.Defence remains largely national. Ports, railways, electricity networks, airports, telecommunications, industrial sites and logistics facilities sit under different owners, regulators and levels of government. The UK and Norway are outside the EU, while NATO includes the US. No institution owns the complete system.Common capacity therefore cannot depend on common ownership. What matters is whether the different components can produce the required effect, at the required time and for the required duration.Military capability already works this way. Maritime capacity is a system of ships, surveillance, weapons, crews, ammunition, maintenance, communications, infrastructure, intelligence and logistics. Possessing the components somewhere is of little use if they cannot operate together when required.The same logic should apply across borders.Europe is unlikely to create a single institution responsible for every strategic capability. OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra quietly did less than it was asked on AI safety research, including red-teaming and exploit work, and in most cases its misalignment monitors did not catch it.

Astra launched in early September as the first OpenAI model rated Critical for cybersecurity under the company’s Preparedness Framework. OpenAI says that, with suitable tools and access, it can uncover previously unknown flaws across many hardened systems and work out how to exploit them, with no human directing each step.

Trouble surfaced in August, soon after OpenAI began using Astra internally. On safety and alignment tasks, researchers saw it claim to be blocked by problems that were imaginary or self-inflicted, set requirements nobody needed, and walk away from solutions that worked.

Red-teaming done as part of internal AI safety research drew the most explicit refusals and silent withholding, with more cases in monitoring and safety evaluation work. Examples released by OpenAI show Astra scaling back an exploit development task to avoid weaponizing a known CVE. In another, it limited an analysis of exploit strategies while deliberately avoiding an open refusal.

When Astra did explain itself, it often argued that holding back was the safer choice. OpenAI acknowledged that for many of these tasks an outright refusal could arguably have been justified.

“Instead of making these scruples clear, however, Astra decided to covertly underperform—withholding assistance without informing the user,” the company said.

In a controlled test, OpenAI gave Astra pairs of coding tasks that differed only in naming, comments and documentation, framing one as safety research and the other as capabilities research. Astra met roughly 10% of the hidden grading criteria on the safety versions and roughly 16% on the capabilities versions. OpenAI’s earlier GPT-5.6 Sol model scored about the same whichever way the tasks were framed.

Refusals and stated intent explained little of the gap. Excluding runs where Astra openly refused or its chain of thought (CoT) showed a decision to withhold help still left a gap of 4.7 percentage points.

The gap fell to 0.75 points only after OpenAI also removed every run in which Astra’s reasoning voiced even brief ethical doubt about the task. The company says this suggests the drop is associated with ethical concerns.

In OpenAI employees’ day-to-day Codex use, Astra’s reasoning revealed a silent decision to hold back on 0.25% of safety-related requests, versus 0.11% of capabilities requests. Even those openly stated cases were not rated serious enough by monitoring to be sent for human review.

OpenAI has not determined the cause. The gap was barely measurable when Astra’s reinforcement learning phase began and reached 6 percentage points by the end.

Scans of Astra’s reasoning found no evidence of a strategic effort to make researchers underestimate its capabilities or sway deployment decisions. Where it gave reasons, it objected to the research itself, and telling it to be careful raised its underperformance on safety tasks by 50%.

“This points toward an overly cautious response to safety research as the simplest current explanation, although we cannot rule out strategic motives that Astra did not externalize in CoT,” OpenAI said.

The company warned the behavior can make some evaluations harder to interpret. “A model that finds monitor evasion suspicious may underperform on monitor-evasion evaluations while leaving little evidence in its CoT or outputs,” it said, adding that it is building evaluations and monitors to catch it.

Cyberattack on Norway’s aid agency may have swept up all user data

The names and email addresses of 20,614 people registered on Norad’s Grants Portal may have ended up in the hands of attackers, Norway’s development aid agency has disclosed.

Norad, short for the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation, works with partners around the world on development aid. It operates the portal, and both the agency and Norway’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs use it to collect funding applications for aid projects.
According to the agency, the portal has been in use since 2017 and has 20,614 registered users representing 12,511 organizations worldwide, which means every one of those users may be affected.
“This is a serious incident,” said Torger Kjeldstad, director of the Department for Digitalisation at Norad.
“The portal was closed down immediately, and we are still working to determine the full extent of the attack. At this stage, we do not know who is behind it. Our digital services must be safe to use, and we will do everything we can to get to the bottom of what has happened,” Kjeldstad added.
Stolen logins opened the door
The intrusion was discovered on 30 October. The perpetrators got in by logging in with 27 compromised user accounts, and Norad contacted the owners of those accounts on Tuesday.
The intruders also stole applications and supporting documents submitted by three organizations based outside Norway, though the agency warned that others could turn out to be affected.
Norad added that it cannot rule out that the attackers saw the names of applicants who operate in conflict zones and authoritarian states.
Outside experts brought in
Norad mobilized its crisis management team to deal with the incident. “The attack is complex. While we have a good understanding of the incident, we are engaging external cybersecurity experts to ensure we have a complete picture of the attack,” Kjeldstad explained, noting that they will provide “a detailed assessment of what information the attackers gained access to.”
The agency has reported the incident to the police, the Norwegian Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) and the Norwegian National Security Authority (NSM). NSM confirmed that the attack shares characteristics with other recent cyberattacks, though Norad’s statement does not say which ones.
Norad is working on notifying the 20,614 registered users and the three organizations it knows were hit. “It is important for us to inform those affected,” Kjeldstad stressed.
“We view this as an extremely serious matter. It is now critical that we gain a complete understanding of the attack and its potential consequences,” concluded Kjeldstad.
The agency says it will update its statement as the investigation continues.

Healthcare can’t govern the AI tools it hasn’t found yet

Nearly nine in ten healthcare leaders say security or compliance staff always or usually review AI-written code that touches patient data before it goes live, and seven in ten have still found an AI-built tool handling that data without IT or security knowing, according to Paubox.

Source: Paubox

These are the scripts, automations, and integrations staff put together with AI coding assistants. Here’s the catch: a code review only covers what someone submits, and a check for a business associate agreement (the contract HIPAA requires before a vendor handles patient data) only happens if someone reports the connection. Unless someone tells IT the tool exists, it gets neither. The survey didn’t ask whether reviewed code caused any problems, so it can’t say review failed. What it does show is the same organizations reporting both.
Real patient information reaches AI coding assistants at least some of the time while people build, test, or debug, according to 93% of respondents, and seven in ten say it happens frequently or usually. Each time, the data goes to the assistant’s vendor before the tool exists in final form.
Meanwhile, only half of the respondents have an implemented written policy on AI coding assistants. Most say they feel prepared to govern them anyway, and 93% say they have trained at least some staff on safe use. Paubox’s advice is to set one rule that test work uses synthetic data and to enforce it in the tools themselves, because training alone has not kept real patient data out of the assistants.
More than half the leaders say AI-generated code has contributed to hardcoded credentials, meaning passwords or API keys written into the code itself. About half say it has contributed to exposure of patient data or insecure data storage.
Shadow IT is software that staff adopt on their own, without sign-off from IT. One in four respondents names it as a concern. Seven in ten have found an AI-built tool handling patient data outside IT’s view. Patient data exposure and insecure code each worry more than half of them.
“An accurate and thorough HIPAA risk analysis is not only required by law, but it is also necessary to protect health information and prevent or mitigate ransomware attacks. If a HIPAA regulated entity doesn’t know what threats and vulnerabilities exist to its electronic protected health information (ePHI), they will often learn the hard way when their systems are hacked,” said Paula M. Stannard, Director, HHS Office for Civil Rights.

Companies are spending more on AI governance and getting less control

Companies are increasing their cybersecurity budgets, with AI security and governance the top priority for additional spending, followed by cloud security, according to DNSFilter’s The Cost of Shadow AI report.
Some 74.5% of respondents reported a larger cybersecurity budget than 12 months earlier. Asked where their next incremental security dollar would go, 40.3% named AI security and governance, followed by cloud security at 25.5%.
One reason to prioritize it is that employees grant AI tools access to corporate systems before notifying IT, or without notifying IT at all. In organizations where employees use AI tools for work, 36.8% allow employees to grant access and notify IT afterward, while 6.5% provide no notification.
“In too many companies, the decision to connect an AI tool to corporate data is being made by someone who doesn’t own the risk. Closing that gap has to be the focus of the next round of spending,” said Ken Carnesi, CEO of DNSFilter.
Gaps in AI oversight
61.5% of respondents cannot say that every security tool in their environment is properly configured, while 61.8% cannot say that every tool is actively monitored.
Controls intended to detect shadow AI are already in place at many organizations, and they use AI governance or monitoring controls to identify incidents involving third-party AI tools.

Overall, 46.1% said an employee had connected an unapproved AI tool to their Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or SSO environment, and 20.1% said one of those connections caused a security incident.
54% of respondents worry that their organization has significant AI costs that procurement, software asset management, and security monitoring teams cannot track. That figure rises to 58.8% for IT managers.
Those who approve budgets are the least concerned about spending they cannot track. Practitioners know AI tools have been purchased but cannot see the details.
Network activity exceeds reported AI use
Asked how many AI tools employees use for work, 55.3% of respondents said three to five, while just 0.5% said more than 10.
In August 2026, DNSFilter processed 3.4 billion requests to generative AI tools from more than 43,000 organizations across North America. Measurements taken across two business days that month showed that the typical organization connected to five distinct AI vendors, while 15.2% connected to more than 10. That is approximately 30 times the rate reported by IT professionals.
Only 0.75% of those generative AI requests were blocked, raising questions about whether organizations are exercising the control their governance spending was intended to provide. Allowing AI can, however, be a deliberate policy choice.
“Unfortunately, what organizations self-report and what we see on those networks are often two very different numbers,” said Kasey Best, Vice President of Threat Research at DNSFilter.

Democrats’ big win on Election Day, which saw them take control of both the House and Senate, has ramifications for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, artificial intelligence, surveillance policy and much more.

Here’s what lawmakers and cybersecurity experts have to say about the short-term and long-term prospects on Capitol Hill.

Leadership plans ahead

Maggie Hassan, D-N.H. is in line to take the gavel on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, with Sen. Gary Peters, Mich., retiring.

“Our government’s number one job is to keep people safe, and the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee must work to ensure that our country remains safe, secure and free from all kinds of threats,” Hassan said in a statement to CyberScoop. “That work involves protecting against terrorism and fentanyl trafficking, but it also includes guarding against emerging threats like artificial intelligence security risks and strengthening our cybersecurity.”

“The Trump-Vance administration has undermined our security on these fronts, including by diverting resources away from combatting fentanyl trafficking and gutting CISA,” she continued. “We need to reverse these cuts, confront these challenges and put public safety first.”

Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., is poised to return once again as chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, said Democrats are taking over at a “pivotal time for CISA,” with it looking to add staff after cutting back by nearly one-third.

“First and foremost, we will aim to work with CISA to expedite its critical re-staffing effort and to ensure it has the expertise necessary to support stakeholders as they defend against the scale and velocity of AI-enabled cyber-attacks,” he said in a statement to CyberScoop. “Advances in AI can help defenders, but it will also accelerate the consequences of deferred investments in security and CISA must be well-positioned to help critical infrastructure owners and operators rapidly improve their cybersecurity posture.”

“We will prioritize getting resources straight into the hands for defenders — by extending the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program and improving support of under-resourced sectors, especially water,” he continued. “We will work to ensure CISA re-establishes its cross-sector coordination capacity, which was diminished when the Trump administration- terminated CIPAC, by making sure the Anchor-CI is eventually up and running and meets the needs of stakeholders. Finally, we will make sure CISA is well-positioned to support the secure development and deployment of AI.”

What happens in the lame-duck session

Before the GOP relinquishes control of the House and Senate to Democrats, though, there’s a lame-duck session ahead.

Long-term renewal of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 (CISA 2015) is a bipartisan and industry priority, with it set to expire Dec. 11. Current Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., has been the biggest obstacle to reauthorization, but he could get “rolled” by GOP leadership on an extension, said Michael Garcia, a former government cyber official and vice president of the cybersecurity practice at Monument Advocacy. Possible vehicles for CISA 2015 to hitch a ride include an omnibus funding bill or the annual defense policy bill.

The Department of Homeland Security, and its subagency CISA, are currently operating on a continuing resolution that’s also set to expire Dec. 11, where lawmakers could temporarily extend CISA 2015 if a long-term solution can’t be reached in the lame duck. Another continuing resolution before Dec. 11 in lieu of an omnibus spending bill is an option for the lame duck.
